name: cosim-vs-embedded-hybrid
title: Process-bigraph co-simulation vs the embedded vcell-fvsolver hybrid solver
description:
The embedded hybrid solver couples its finite volume PDE solver to a VCell-patched
Smoldyn 2.38 through lagged operator splitting (see docs/fvsolver-hybrid-notes.md):

- Each side reads the other's state from the previous step.
- Particle counts are binned to the nearest grid node.
- Field-dependent particle reaction rates are looked up from the containing voxel.

This investigation rebuilds that method from two independent process-bigraph
processes and compares the result against the embedded solver: first the units and
binning handoff, then the reaction classes in order of coupling difficulty, then
convergence and performance.

Coupling-semantics note (Phase 0): process-bigraph reads state at the start of each
interval, which matches fvsolver for the PDE side. A Smoldyn step of k·dt in fvsolver
reads the field at T+(k-1)·dt, not at T. To replicate that exactly, the Smoldyn
process runs on the PDE clock and steps every k-th call
(tests/test_scheduling_semantics.py).

at_a_glance.role: Pure diffusion on each side plus the histogram-to-concentration handoff; checks units, boundary volumes and conservation.
A_particle -> 0 at rate k·[B](x): the simplest field-to-particle coupling, against the analytic and continuum limit.
A_particle -> B_field and 0th-order 0 -> A_particle at rate k·[B]: mass balance across the handoff in both directions.
A_particle + B_field -> C_field: per-region ensemble mean and variance, co-sim vs fvsolver.
Sweeps the Smoldyn step multiplier k and dt; compares error curves of both implementations.
Wall time vs grid size, particle count and k, with a per-component overhead breakdown.

question: Can a process-bigraph co-simulation of a PDE process and a Smoldyn process reproduce the hybrid PDE/particle solver embedded in vcell-fvsolver to within its stochastic error, and at what computational cost?
hypothesis: With the same Cartesian mesh, the same nearest-node binning and units, and the same lagged explicit coupling, the co-simulation's ensemble statistics are statistically indistinguishable from fvsolver's. The co-simulation is slower by a bounded per-coupling-step overhead (scheduling plus data marshaling), and both converge at first order in the coupling interval.

executive.what_is_this: A head-to-head comparison of a modular (process-bigraph) and a hard-coded (vcell-fvsolver) implementation of the same PDE/particle hybrid algorithm.
executive.verdict:
Yes. The process-bigraph co-simulation reproduces the embedded vcell-fvsolver hybrid to within its stochastic error on every like-for-like test, with the same first-order coupling error. - A2: field-to-particle coupling, |z| < 2.6. - A4: two-way bimolecular coupling, |z| < 2.1. - A5: coupling error 1.05× the native error at k = 16. It is also faster: 0.25–0.93× of the native solve time (A6). Where they differ, the native solver is wrong: - A3: boundary cells overproduce field-dependent particle creation by Σfull/Σactual
  (virtualcell/vcell-fvsolver#24).
- VCell math generation keeps no-op particle processes (virtualcell/vcell#2158). - A second hybrid solve in one process segfaults (vcell-fvsolver#23). - The native solver crashes at a large step multiplier. The co-simulation's "start-of-interval" scheduling halves the coupling error at large k. vcell-fvsolver's hybrid loop fixes a single splitting order.

studies.name: handoff-units-and-binning
studies.title: Each side alone, and the particle-to-grid handoff
studies.question:
Before coupling anything: does each half of the co-simulation behave correctly on its own,
and does the particle-to-grid handoff (nearest-node binning, boundary element volumes,
counts to µM) follow vcell-fvsolver's conventions?

findings.statement: Each half of the co-simulation is correct in isolation: the FV operator reproduces the analytic cosine-mode decay to 6.0e-4 relative error, and Smoldyn's binned per-axis variance (dx²/6-corrected) matches 2Dt to 0.13% relative error at t=1 s.
findings.next_action: None — both solvers verified against their continuum limits.

findings.statement: The particle-to-grid handoff is exact and volume-correct: the histogram total never differs from the molecule count (mismatch = 0 molecules at every record), and uniformly distributed particles bin to a uniform concentration across node classes (max |z| = 0.48; corner and edge concentrations 1.0034× and 1.0019× interior, both within 0.4%), confirming the 1/4-corner and 1/2-edge element-volume convention.
findings.next_action: Proceed to the coupled field-modulated-decay study (pipeline gate satisfied).

biological_validation.basis: Numerical-convergence study: each half matches its continuum/theoretical limit — FV vs analytic diffusion and binned particle variance vs 2Dt (free Brownian motion).

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all four primary behavior tests pass against it (FV err 6.0e-4, variance err 0.13%, histogram mismatch 0, boundary max|z| 0.48).

explanatory_gain.basis: Localizes correctness to the handoff itself: molecule conservation is exact and the boundary element-volume convention (corner 1/4, edge 1/2) yields a uniform binned concentration, so the production composite's particle→grid path is sound.

derived.insight: Each half of the co-simulation is correct in isolation: the FV operator reproduces the analytic cosine-mode decay to 6.0e-4 relative error, and Smoldyn's binned per-axis variance (dx²/6-corrected) matches 2Dt to 0.13% relative error at t=1 s.

studies.name: field-modulated-decay
studies.title: Field-to-particle coupling, A_particle -> 0 at rate k·[B](x)
studies.question:
Does the Smoldyn process read the PDE field at each molecule as vcell-fvsolver does
(nearest node, value from the previous coupling step)? Does the coupled model approach
its deterministic continuum limit?

findings.statement: The particle side reads the PDE field correctly: with static B and immobile A, per- column survival matches N0·exp(-k·B_col·t) with max |z| = 1.56 (co-sim) and 1.68 (native VCell), both well under the |z| < 4 band, and exactly zero molecules decay in the B = 0 column.
findings.next_action: None — field read confirmed against the exact expectation on both solvers.

findings.statement: The coupled model converges to its deterministic continuum limit: with diffusing A and a Gaussian B, the ensemble-mean A is within 2.7% relative L2 (band 6%) and the total A within 0.05% (band 2%) of the all-continuous FV solution — both at the sampling-noise level.

The co-simulation and VCell's native hybrid are statistically indistinguishable on this field-to-particle coupling: static-field survival agrees at max |z| = 1.37, the diffusing final x-profiles at |z| = 2.54, and total survival to 0.04%, with the B fields identical to 1e-16 — so GridValueProvider's nearest-node field read is reproduced by the process-bigraph decomposition.
findings.next_action: Clears the pipeline gate to two-way-exchange; no further action for this model.

biological_validation.basis: Per-column survival matches the exact exp(-k·B·t) expectation (|z|=1.56) with no decay where B=0, and the coupled model converges to the continuum FV solution within 2.7% L2.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all eight behavior tests pass (static |z|=1.56, native |z|=1.68, continuum L2 2.7%, cosim-vs-native profile |z|=2.54).

explanatory_gain.basis: F-03 shows the process-bigraph decomposition reproduces VCell's nearest-node GridValueProvider field read (B fields identical to 1e-16; survival/profile agreement within sampling), validating the headless native reference path.

derived.insight: The particle side reads the PDE field correctly: with static B and immobile A, per- column survival matches N0·exp(-k·B_col·t) with max |z| = 1.56 (co-sim) and 1.68 (native VCell), both well under the |z| < 4 band, and exactly zero molecules decay in the B = 0 column.

studies.name: two-way-exchange
studies.title: Mass balance across the particle ↔ field handoff
studies.question:
When molecules move both ways between particle and field representations (A_particle
→ B_field and B_field → A_particle by field-dependent creation), is total A + B
conserved and is the right steady state reached? Do both solvers agree?

findings.statement: The co-simulation conserves mass and reaches the right steady state across the two-way handoff: ensemble-mean (A+B) stays within 1.18% of its initial value over 5 s, and the late-time total-A/total-B ratio is within 0.32% of k2/k1 (16 seeds).
findings.next_action: None — mass balance and detailed balance confirmed for the co-simulation.

findings.statement: Field-dependent creation in the co-simulation is exact: created A is 0.994× the exact expectation k2·[B]·V·602.214·t (creation-only, static B), confirming that using each node's actual cell volume (1/2–1/8 at boundaries) removes the overproduction; the 0.6% shortfall is the ~2-step Smoldyn creation start-up artifact.
findings.next_action: None — boundary-volume and skipped-node defects fixed in the Smoldyn fork.

findings.statement: The native VCell embedded solver diverges strongly and the divergence is fully explained by a known defect: native creation is 1.813× the expectation, matching the predicted full-volume boundary overproduction Σ(full)/Σ(actual)=1.815× to 0.1% (ratio 0.999). As a consequence native (A+B) grows 177% in 5 s and its steady-state ratio is 51% off, so the two solvers disagree at |z| ≈ 219 (totals) / 153 (profile). This is vcell-fvsolver's bug (virtualcell/vcell-fvsolver#24), not the coupling method.
findings.next_action: Carry the boundary-volume fix upstream to vcell-fvsolver; once fixed, replace this characterization test with a native mass-balance test.

biological_validation.basis: Theoretical targets met: A+B conservation in expectation, detailed-balance steady state at k2/k1, and the exact field-dependent creation rate k2·[B]·V·602.214·t for the co-simulation.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all three primary co-sim tests pass (mass balance 1.18%, steady ratio 0.32%, creation 0.994×), and the secondary native-defect characterization passes (0.999).

explanatory_gain.basis: Separates coupling from engine defect: the co-simulation is exact, while the native solver's 1.813× creation is quantitatively explained by full-volume boundary overproduction (predicted 1.815×), isolating the bug to vcell-fvsolver#24.

derived.insight: The co-simulation conserves mass and reaches the right steady state across the two-way handoff: ensemble-mean (A+B) stays within 1.18% of its initial value over 5 s, and the late-time total-A/total-B ratio is within 0.32% of k2/k1 (16 seeds).

studies.name: bimolecular-hybrid
studies.title: A_particle + B_field → C_field: two-way nonlinear coupling, both solvers
studies.question:
When particles consume a field (B substantially depleted by A), do the co-simulation
and the native VCell hybrid agree with each other and with the deterministic continuum
limit?

findings.statement: The co-simulation and the native VCell hybrid agree to within sampling on the two-way nonlinear coupling: max-over-time |z| is 1.79 for surviving A fraction, 0.85 for produced C, and 2.10 for the final x-profile — all well under the |z| < 4 threshold.
findings.next_action: None — the two solvers are statistically indistinguishable on this model.

findings.statement: Both solvers approach the deterministic continuum limit at 20,000 particles: the max-over-time absolute survival difference is 0.29% (co-sim) and 0.18% (native), both under the 1% band. The remainder is explicit-coupling lag plus discreteness.

B + C is conserved to round-off on the PDE side in both solvers (max relative deviation 3.6e-14 co-sim, 3.2e-14 native), confirming the particle-consumption / field-production handoff is mass-balanced. Reaching this agreement exposed and fixed a float-sum record-time bug in process-bigraph (pre-fix survival |z| = 5.9, C |z| = 71).
findings.next_action: Carry the half-step record-time fix as a regression pin; no further action for this model.

biological_validation.basis: Both the co-simulation and the native VCell hybrid converge to the deterministic continuum solution of the two-way bimolecular model to within ~0.3% absolute survival.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all four behavior tests pass against it (survival |z|=1.79, C |z|=0.85, co-sim continuum 0.29%, native continuum 0.18%).

explanatory_gain.basis: F-03 localizes a float-sum record-time bug exposed by this nonlinear coupling (pre-fix |z|=71 on C), and shows the fixed process-bigraph decomposition is answer-preserving with exact B+C conservation.

derived.insight: The co-simulation and the native VCell hybrid agree to within sampling on the two-way nonlinear coupling: max-over-time |z| is 1.79 for surviving A fraction, 0.85 for produced C, and 2.10 for the final x-profile — all well under the |z| < 4 threshold.

studies.name: coupling-interval-convergence
studies.title: Coupling error vs Smoldyn step multiplier, co-simulation (two schemes) and native VCell
studies.question:
How does the error of the lagged explicit coupling grow with the coupling interval
k·Δt (Smoldyn steps once per k PDE steps)? Does the co-simulation reproduce
fvsolver's coupling error, and does process-bigraph's plain scheduling
("start-of-interval") do better or worse?

findings.statement: The lagged explicit coupling is first order in the coupling interval k·Δt on both fvsolver-semantics solvers: fitted order (k ≥ 4) is 1.23 (co-sim fvsolver mode) and 1.07 (native), both inside the theoretical [0.7, 1.5] band.
findings.next_action: None — convergence order confirmed on both solvers.

findings.statement: The co-simulation reproduces the embedded solver's coupling error, not just its results: at k = 16 (0.08 s) the co-sim fvsolver-mode error is 0.0110 and the native error 0.0104, a ratio of 1.05 (band [0.8, 1.25]).

Plain process-bigraph "start-of-interval" scheduling roughly halves the coupling error at large k (0.0049 at k=16, 0.0110 at k=32 vs 0.0110 and 0.0218 for fvsolver mode; fitted order 0.80), because reading the field at the start of the particle step partly cancels the PDE side's lag. vcell-fvsolver's fixed ordering cannot use this without changing the solver.
findings.next_action: Pursue higher-order operator splitting in Investigation B; the native solver crashes at k=32 (Smoldyn step equal to the output interval), so its sweep stops at k=16.

biological_validation.basis: Both fvsolver-semantics solvers show the expected first-order error in the coupling interval k·Δt, matching explicit-lagged operator-splitting theory.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all three primary behavior tests pass (co-sim order 1.23, native order 1.07, k=16 ratio 1.05).

explanatory_gain.basis: F-02 shows the co-simulation reproduces the embedded solver's coupling error to within 5%, and F-03 quantifies how an alternate scheduling scheme (start-of-interval) halves that error — a design lever unavailable to the fixed native loop.

derived.insight: The lagged explicit coupling is first order in the coupling interval k·Δt on both fvsolver-semantics solvers: fitted order (k ≥ 4) is 1.23 (co-sim fvsolver mode) and 1.07 (native), both inside the theoretical [0.7, 1.5] band.

studies.name: performance-scaling
studies.title: Wall time of the co-simulation vs the native VCell hybrid, with breakdown
studies.question:
What does decomposing the hybrid solver into process-bigraph processes cost? How does
the co-simulation's wall time compare with the native embedded solver as the grid and
the particle count grow, and how much of it is framework overhead?

findings.statement: The process-bigraph framework overhead is bounded and small: at most 2.97 milliseconds per step across all configurations (the bound is 10 milliseconds), ranging from 3.5% of co-sim time on the heaviest problem (200k particles) up to 41.7% on the smallest (2k particles on 21×21×3), where there is little real work to amortize it against.
findings.next_action: None — overhead confirmed bounded; watch it only for very small, many-step problems.

findings.statement: The modular co-simulation is faster than the native embedded solve in every configuration: co-sim/native-solve ranges from 0.25× (2k particles) to 0.93× on the largest grid (81×81×3), and 0.69× at 200k particles (co-sim 2.64 s vs native solve 3.82 s). The decomposition costs nothing at scale — well under the 2× bound.
findings.next_action: None — likely from Smoldyn 2.7x vs 2.38, direct sparse LU vs PCG, and VCell's per-output writes.

findings.statement: Co-sim time shifts cleanly with the workload: particles dominate at high particle counts (95.9% of co-sim time at 200k particles, PDE only 0.8%), while the PDE dominates on the largest grid (49.7% at 81×81×3). Framework overhead is largest precisely where total work is smallest (41.7% at 2k particles), as expected for a fixed per-step scheduling cost.

biological_validation.basis: N/A — performance study; see regression_compatibility. No biological claim is made; the measurements are wall-time and throughput.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; both behavior tests pass (framework overhead max 2.97 ms/step < 10; largest-grid co-sim/native 0.93× < 2.0).

explanatory_gain.basis: Attributes co-sim cost to its parts: particles dominate at high particle counts (95.9% at 200k), the PDE on the largest grid (49.7% at 81×81×3), and fixed per-step framework overhead (≤ 2.97 ms) matters only for the smallest problems.

derived.insight: The process-bigraph framework overhead is bounded and small: at most 2.97 milliseconds per step across all configurations (the bound is 10 milliseconds), ranging from 3.5% of co-sim time on the heaviest problem (200k particles) up to 41.7% on the smallest (2k particles on 21×21×3), where there is little real work to amortize it against.
